data.title: Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) — viva
data.summary: Vascular & ulcers · 10 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis)** (Vascular & ulcers)_

**Q1. Define IgA vasculitis (HSP).**
- Small-vessel vasculitis with IgA1-dominant immune deposits affecting skin, joints, gut and kidneys; commonest systemic vasculitis of childhood (3–15 y, peak 4–6), often after upper respiratory infection (group A streptococcus); adults have more renal disease

**Q2. Classify vasculitis (PYQ) — Chapel Hill 2012.**
- Large vessel: Takayasu arteritis, giant cell arteritis
- Medium vessel: polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease
- Small vessel — ANCA-associated: microscopic polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's), eosinophilic GPA (Churg–Strauss); immune-complex: anti-GBM disease, cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis, IgA vasculitis (HSP), hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis (anti-C1q)
- Variable vessel: Behçet's, Cogan's syndrome
- Single-organ: cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis, cutaneous arteritis, primary CNS vasculitis
- Vasculitis associated with systemic disease (lupus, RA, sarcoid) and with probable aetiology (hepatitis B PAN, hepatitis C cryoglobulinaemia, drug-associated, cancer-associated)

**Q3. Give the EULAR/PRINTO/PRES classification criteria.**
- Mandatory: purpura or petechiae with lower-limb predominance (non-thrombocytopenic)
- Plus ≥1 of: diffuse abdominal pain; histopathology showing leukocytoclastic vasculitis or proliferative glomerulonephritis with predominant IgA deposits; arthritis or arthralgia; renal involvement (proteinuria >0.3 g/24 h or haematuria/red cell casts)

**Q4. Describe the clinical features.**
- Skin (100%): palpable purpura — symmetrical on buttocks, extensor lower limbs, ankles (dependent areas); starts as urticarial/erythematous papules; may become bullous, haemorrhagic, necrotic; oedema of scalp, face, hands, scrotum in young children
- Joints (75%): transient arthralgia/arthritis of knees and ankles, non-deforming
- GI (50–75%): colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, GI bleed (melaena), intussusception (ileo-ileal), bowel perforation
- Renal (20–50%): microscopic haematuria, proteinuria, nephritic/nephrotic syndrome — determines long-term prognosis (ESRD in 1–2% children, more in adults)
- Others: orchitis (mimics torsion), CNS vasculitis, pulmonary haemorrhage (rare)

**Q5. Classify purpura (PYQ).**
- Non-palpable (haemorrhage without vessel inflammation): thrombocytopenic (ITP, TTP, marrow failure, DIC), platelet dysfunction, coagulation defects, vascular fragility (senile/actinic purpura, steroid purpura, scurvy — perifollicular haemorrhage with corkscrew hairs, Ehlers–Danlos, amyloidosis — pinch purpura), raised intravascular pressure (cough, vomiting), pigmented purpuric dermatoses
- Palpable (inflammatory — vasculitis): leukocytoclastic vasculitis, IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemia, urticarial vasculitis
- Retiform/net-like (occlusion of vessels): APS, cryoglobulinaemia type I, calciphylaxis, purpura fulminans, warfarin/heparin necrosis, septic emboli, cholesterol emboli, levamisole-adulterated cocaine

**Q6. Discuss the evaluation of vasculitis (PYQ).**
- Confirm vasculitis: skin biopsy from a fresh (<24–48 h) lesion for histology + DIF (IgA in vessel walls in HSP — best in lesions <48 h old)
- Assess extent: urine dipstick and microscopy (haematuria, casts), urine protein:creatinine ratio, serum creatinine, BP; stool occult blood, abdominal ultrasound (intussusception) if pain; chest X-ray; nerve conduction if neuropathy
- Find cause: CBC, ESR/CRP, ASO, throat swab, hepatitis B/C, HIV, ANA, anti-dsDNA, RF, C3/C4, cryoglobulins, ANCA (MPO, PR3), serum IgA (raised in 50%), serum protein electrophoresis, drug history, malignancy screen in adults

**Q7. Histopathology.**
- Leukocytoclastic vasculitis of superficial dermal post-capillary venules: fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls, neutrophils with nuclear dust (leukocytoclasia), extravasated RBCs, endothelial swelling
- DIF: granular IgA (± C3) deposits in vessel walls — key differentiating feature
- Kidney: mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis with mesangial IgA (same as IgA nephropathy)

**Q8. Differential diagnosis.**
- Other small-vessel vasculitis (hypersensitivity/drug, cryoglobulinaemia, urticarial vasculitis, ANCA), acute haemorrhagic oedema of infancy (large rosette/cockade purpura on face and limbs of well infant <2 y, self-limiting), ITP (non-palpable), meningococcaemia (sick child, retiform purpura — emergency), child abuse, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, septic emboli

**Q9. Management.**
- Mostly self-limiting (4–6 weeks): rest, leg elevation, compression; NSAIDs/paracetamol for arthralgia (avoid NSAIDs if renal involvement)
- Severe abdominal pain, scrotal involvement, extensive necrotic skin: systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day) — relieve GI/joint symptoms; do not prevent nephritis
- Renal disease (proteinuria, nephrotic, crescentic GN): steroids (pulse methylprednisolone) + azathioprine/mycophenolate/cyclophosphamide; ACE inhibitors for proteinuria; nephrology follow-up
- Skin-only chronic: dapsone, colchicine
- Urine monitoring (dipstick and BP) weekly for the first month, then monthly up to 6–12 months — nephritis can appear late

**Q10. Prognosis.**
- Excellent in most children; recurrences in ~1/3 within months; long-term outcome depends on renal involvement — worse in adults, nephrotic range proteinuria, crescents on biopsy

## Quick spotter facts
- Palpable purpura on buttocks/legs + abdominal pain + arthritis + haematuria in a child — IgA vasculitis
- DIF: IgA in vessel walls
- Monitor urine for 6–12 months

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Cutaneous vasculitis); 2012 Chapel Hill nomenclature; EULAR/PRINTO/PRES 2010 criteria. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
